The Parlor is an independent publication documenting grassroots initiatives, community-led solutions, and the people building them.

We are interested in stories that highlight how individuals and communities respond to social challenges through organizing, collaboration, and experimentation.

Our goal is to create a digital meeting space where movements, organizers, and thinkers encounter each other’s work.

We prioritize storytelling that centers real people, real communities, and real initiatives.

Submissions and freelance collaborations are currently closed while we focus on fulfilling our existing financial commitments to writers and contributors. Please check back here for news of future pitching and publishing opportunities.

Our Editorial Verticals

Perspectives & IdentityWorld & PoliticsSociety & CultureWork & Wealth

We publish across our editorial verticals, exploring politics, culture, identity, work, and economic life through the experiences of real people and communities.

Occasionally, we also publish seasonal issues and collections. For these, we publish a call for submissions with specific guidelines and themes.

Explore our latest issue.

Perspectives & Identity

Human-interest stories and personal essays that explore how identity, lived experience, and community shape the way people navigate social and political realities.

These pieces should offer insight into how individuals experience and respond to broader social issues, particularly within marginalized or underrepresented communities.

We are especially interested in essays that connect personal narrative to:

  • community belonging
  • cultural identity
  • migration and diaspora
  • gender and feminist experiences
  • intergenerational stories
  • Kinship and family dynamics
  • Personal experiences of organizing or activism

World & Politics

This section examines how political decisions, laws, and geopolitical developments shape the lives of real communities.

Rather than focusing on traditional political commentary, we prioritize reporting and interviews that explore politics from the ground up.

Stories may include:

  • local political movements and civic organizing
  • community responses to policy decisions
  • organizers working to influence legislation
  • grassroots political campaigns
  • cross-border solidarity networks
  • interviews with activists and policymakers
  • geopolitical developments examined through the experiences of affected communities

Our goal is to understand politics through the people living its consequences and shaping its outcomes.

Society & Culture

This section explores the social and cultural forces shaping communities.

We focus on stories that highlight how people create meaning, build relationships, and organize within their cultural environments.

Topics may include:

  • local cultural movements and social trends
  • artists, musicians, and cultural workers shaping their communities
  • theatre, literature, and creative spaces tied to social change
  • cultural identity and community storytelling
  • Profiles on Authors about their books and researchers about their work

These pieces examine how culture both reflects and drives social transformation.

Work & Wealth

This section explores alternative economic pathways and financial empowerment within underrepresented communities.

We prioritize stories about:

  • women, BIPOC, and LGBTQ+ entrepreneurs
  • cooperative or community-owned businesses
  • creators building unconventional revenue streams
  • mutual aid and alternative economic systems
  • financial literacy and wealth-building strategies for marginalized communities

What We Do Not Publish

To maintain a clear editorial focus, we generally do not publish:

  • General Opinion Commentary — Opinion pieces that are not connected to specific communities, initiatives, or organizing efforts.
  • Trend or Culture Analysis — Articles focused primarily on social media trends, celebrity culture, wellness fads, or pop culture commentary.
  • Abstract Political Commentary — Political analysis that is not grounded in reporting on real communities or movements.
  • Lifestyle or Consumer Culture — Stories centered on fashion, beauty, consumer products, or lifestyle trends.
  • Personal Essays Without Broader Context — Personal reflections that do not engage with community, identity, or social issues.

Before You Pitch

Overview

Ask yourself:

  • Does this story highlight a community initiative or organizing effort?
  • Does it center people building something in the world?
  • Does it explore identity, lived experience, or community in a meaningful way?

If the answer is yes, your story may be a good fit for The Parlor. Please check the submissions notice above for current opportunities.

AI Use Policy

  • Human judgment and responsibility — The Parlor is a publication made by people. Writers and editors remain responsible for the accuracy, originality, fairness, and integrity of everything we publish. An AI tool is not a source, a reporter, or a substitute for editorial judgment.
  • Limited assistive uses — With editorial oversight, AI tools may assist with tasks such as transcription, translation, spelling and grammar checks, accessibility, and organizing material. Transcripts must be checked against the original recording; translations must be reviewed by someone competent in the relevant language. Substantive changes require human review. These tools must not replace original reporting or the author's own writing and analysis.
  • Reporting and verification — We do not publish AI-generated articles or personal testimony presented as a person's lived experience. We do not use AI to fabricate quotations, sources, interviews, events, citations, or research findings. Any factual suggestion from an AI tool must be independently verified against reliable original sources before use. AI output must never be treated as evidence.
  • Images, audio, and video — We do not use AI-generated or materially AI-altered images, audio, or video as documentary evidence of real people, places, or events. Any permitted use of generative AI for illustration must receive editorial approval, be clearly labeled, and be distinguishable from documentary material. Routine technical adjustments must not change the meaning or factual content of an image or recording.
  • Privacy, consent, and creative rights — Confidential source material, unpublished submissions, personal data, and sensitive recordings must not be entered into external AI services without editorial approval and an assessment of consent, confidentiality, security, and the service's data-retention and training terms. We do not use AI to impersonate people or reproduce another creator's work without appropriate permission.
  • Disclosure — Contributors must tell their editor how AI was used in preparing a submission. When an approved AI use materially shapes published content, we explain its role to readers in a note accompanying the work. Routine spelling and grammar checks alone do not require a public note.
  • Accountability and review — Human editors make publication decisions. Errors involving AI-assisted work are subject to the same correction standards as other errors. We will review this policy as tools and their implications change.
